title: B-tree
summary: B-trees are self-balancing tree data structures that maintain sorted data and allow logarithmic-time searches, sequential access, insertions, and deletions. This web page explains their definition, history, complexities, operational algorithms, variants, and widespread usage in databases and filesystems.
tags: data structures, databases, filesystems, algorithms

title: Hash table
summary: Hash tables are data structures that implement associative arrays by mapping keys to values using hash functions. This web page explains their time and space complexity, history, load factor management, hash function design, collision resolution techniques, dynamic resizing, and practical applications.
tags: algorithms, hash tables, data structures, hashing

title: Database index
summary: Database indexes are data structures that improve the speed of data retrieval operations on a table at the cost of additional writes and storage space. They enable fast lookups, help police database constraints, and can be structured in several ways depending on performance needs.
tags: databases, algorithms, data structures, hashing

title: Log-structured merge-tree
summary: Log-structured merge-tree is a data structure designed to provide high-performance indexed access for files with large insert volumes, such as transaction logs. It maintains key-value pairs across multiple separate structures optimized for different storage mediums, synchronizing data efficiently in batches.
tags: data structures, algorithms, storage systems

title: Bloom filter
summary: Bloom filters are space-efficient probabilistic data structures used to test set membership with a risk of false positives but no false negatives. This web page explains their algorithms, space and time advantages, probability mathematics, and various practical applications in computer science.
tags: algorithms, databases, storage systems

title: Raft (algorithm)
summary: Raft is a consensus algorithm designed as an understandable alternative to Paxos for distributing a state machine across a cluster of computing systems. It achieves consensus through a single elected leader that manages log replication, safety properties, and cluster membership changes.
tags: consensus algorithms, distributed systems, log replication, fault tolerance

title: Paxos (computer science)
summary: Paxos is a family of consensus protocols used to achieve agreement on a single result among a group of unreliable processors. It forms the basis of state machine replication, ensuring safety and fault tolerance in distributed computing systems.
tags: distributed systems, consensus algorithms, fault tolerance, storage systems, algorithms

title: CAP theorem
summary: The CAP theorem states that any distributed data store can provide at most two of three guarantees: consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. It explains the trade-offs system designers must make when network partitions occur.
tags: distributed systems, databases, fault tolerance, storage systems

title: Consistent hashing
summary: Consistent hashing is a specialized hashing technique designed to evenly distribute keys across shards or servers while minimizing key remapping when the system changes size. It is widely used in distributed caching, content delivery networks, and databases to maintain stability during server additions or failures.
tags: algorithms, distributed systems, hash tables, storage systems

title: Two-phase commit protocol
summary: The two-phase commit protocol is a distributed algorithm used in transaction processing and databases to coordinate whether participating processes should commit or abort an atomic transaction. This web page explains its normal execution phases, underlying assumptions, basic algorithm, disadvantages, common architecture, and various protocol optimizations.
tags: distributed systems, databases, consensus algorithms, algorithms, storage systems

title: Transformer (deep learning)
summary: Transformers are an artificial neural network architecture based on the multi-head attention mechanism that process entire input sequences in parallel using embedding and attention layers. This web page explains their history, core architectural components, training stabilization techniques, variants, and various applications across natural language processing and other domains.
tags: algorithms, neural networks, deep learning, machine learning, natural language processing

title: Attention (machine learning)
summary: Attention in machine learning is a method that determines the importance of each component in a sequence relative to others. This overview details the history, variants, mathematical formulations, and applications of attention mechanisms in deep learning.
tags: machine learning, neural networks, deep learning, algorithms

title: Word2Vec
summary: Word2Vec explains a technique in natural language processing for generating vector representations of words as word embeddings based on surrounding text context. It covers the continuous bag of words and skip-gram architectures, mathematical details, historical context, parameterization, and various extensions.
tags: natural language processing, neural networks, deep learning, algorithms

title: BERT (language model)
summary: BERT is a bidirectional encoder-only transformer language model introduced by Google in 2018 that represents text as token vectors through self-supervised learning. It is trained via masked token prediction and next sentence prediction to generate contextualized word representations that improve natural language processing tasks. The web page provides a comprehensive overview of its architecture, training methods, historical development, and downstream fine-tuning applications.
tags: deep learning, natural language processing, neural networks, machine learning

title: Retrieval-augmented generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation is a technique that enables large language models to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources to improve factual accuracy. This web page outlines the core mechanisms, stages, applications, improvements, and challenges associated with the technology, including limitations like hallucination and risks such as RAG poisoning.
tags: deep learning, neural networks, databases, storage systems, algorithms

title: TCP congestion control
summary: Transmission Control Protocol congestion control strategies, algorithms, and mechanisms are used to prevent network congestion and avoid congestive collapse. Foundational approaches like AIMD, slow start, and fast retransmit are detailed alongside modern variations such as CUBIC, BBR, and network-assisted schemes.
tags: algorithms, deep learning, distributed systems, fault tolerance, networking

title: HTTP/2
summary: HTTP/2 is a major revision of the HTTP network protocol designed to decrease latency and improve web page loading speeds. Derived from Google's experimental SPDY protocol, it was developed by the IETF HTTP Working Group and published in 2015.
tags: networking, storage systems, distributed systems

title: Garbage collection (computer science)
summary: Garbage collection is a form of automatic memory management that reclaims memory allocated by a program which is no longer referenced. Invented around 1959 by John McCarthy to simplify Lisp, it relieves programmers from manual memory de-allocation while introducing performance overhead.
tags: algorithms, deep learning, storage systems, memory management

title: Dijkstra's algorithm
summary: Dijkstra's algorithm is a classic graph search method that computes the shortest path between nodes in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. Conceived by Edsger W. Dijkstra, the algorithm iteratively explores unvisited neighbors using a priority queue to determine optimal routes.
tags: algorithms, graph algorithms, shortest path, greedy algorithms, dynamic programming

title: Public-key cryptography
summary: Public-key cryptography explains how cryptographic systems use pairs of related public and private keys to secure electronic communications and data storage. This web page outlines the core mechanisms, historical development, applications, and potential vulnerabilities associated with asymmetric cryptographic algorithms.
tags: asymmetric cryptography, security protocols, encryption algorithms, digital signatures, cryptographic history
